articles.title_orig: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
articles.title_zh: Warby Parker bets on Google AI glasses for growth, but privacy fears still loom
articles.content_orig:
Google and Samsung's next face computers have arrived. Nearly two years after the companies first announced the Android XR platform that powers the hardware, the smart glasses are finally on sale.
The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform. Smart glasses are just one part of Android XR—there are also mixed-reality headsets and glasses for more immersive experiences, like last year's Samsung Galaxy XR and the upcoming Xreal Aura .
Eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are heavily involved in the new smart glasses, responsible for the design and fit, similar to how Meta tapped Ray-Ban for its competing—and market-leading—wearables. Google and Samsung are leveraging Warby Parker and Gentle Monster's brick-and-mortar presence and retail expertise, which lets people demo the glasses before buying them. (Kering Eyewear, which owns brands like Lindberg and Maui Jim, has also signed up to make glasses for Android XR in the future.)
The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10. Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and come in three styles—Alden, Reid, and Wren—as optical or sunglasses, with various prescription, lens, and width options. Gentle Monster's glasses start at $449 and come in six designs, various colors, and tints, with prescription options for most frames.
The hardware is identical across both brands. The glasses weigh around 41 grams (10 grams less than Meta's new Gen 3 glasses ), have a nine-hour battery life, and include a charging case that can recharge the glasses up to seven times. They have a 12-megapixel camera with an LED indicator that shows everyone in eyeshot that you’re recording. There’s a button to capture photos and 90-second videos at up to 3K resolution with a press. A touch-sensitive temple piece lets you tap to activate the onboard Gemini assistant, or slide two fingers back and forth to control the volume of the audio coming out of the glasses' speaker.
They are the first devices to support the “Hey Gemini” hotword, though you can use the well-known “Hey Google” hotword if you'd like. Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR.
“We felt that these are a Gemini-forward device,” Payne tells WIRED. “It's really you and Gemini going through your day together, so it was feeling a little dissonant for us. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.”
Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices— Google Pixel phones , Samsung Galaxy phones , and iPhones —and only select models. You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer. A Google spokesperson tells WIRED the company will share more about how it plans to expand support to other phones in 2027 after launch.
The arms of the glasses are similarly thick.
Since you'll be buying the glasses from an eyewear brand, they will be the customer-facing party to handle any problems you may have with the device or prescriptions. On the backend, Payne says there are elaborate business integrations and handoffs, so the customer service workload is split between all the companies.
Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues. However, they are not ready yet; Payne says they're currently being tested by “non-Googlers” and are still on the road map, though he didn't share a specific release window. As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio , Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.”
Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms. Unlike display smart glasses designed to plug into a laptop to mirror or extend your screen, or more immersive glasses like Meta's VR Glasses , which layer virtual experiences over the real world, Intelligent Eyewear is more akin to what Google pitched years ago with the original Google Glass .
You can hear notifications pipe through from your connected smartphone and respond to messages by speaking to Gemini. You can listen to music, take phone calls, and get audio navigation through Google Maps. Yes, you can snap photos and videos too, though Payne quickly notes that these glasses are designed more to have Gemini assist you throughout the day than to capture content.
That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “ Glasshole ”).
“We learned through Glass that you can make people uncomfortable if you're not clearly communicating,” Payne says.
To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns. They include tamper detection, so the camera will know if you tried to disable the indicator light. If you try to block the indicator light while recording, the camera will stop. When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads. The glasses will automatically redact the faces of people around you before Gemini processes the visual data. We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story .
Gentle Monster's Intelligent Eyewear comes in six different styles.
Most of the features that Google is positioning around Intelligent Eyewear rely on Gemini. See a poster for a comedy show? Just ask Gemini for more information, or add it to your calendar. You can ask Gemini to add items to your shopping list or whip up a travel itinerary with hotel recommendations and save them to a note. Some of these are saved in the Gemini app, but it can leverage other apps on your smartphone. For example, Gemini can play music on Apple Music if you're on an iPhone. And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved.
When you activate Gemini, it's technically a “ Gemini Live ” experience, meaning the assistant activates and you can have a free-flowing conversation. A swipe back on the glasses' arm will end the interaction. When you want it to “look” at something in front of you, be specific in your query; otherwise, it won't use the camera. You can ask it to look at a page in a book and summarize the content, or if you have a bunch of cocktail ingredients in front of you but don't know what to make, you can ask Gemini for suggestions and step-by-step instructions to craft a drink—at your pace.
Some Gemini controls are on-device and don't need to travel to the cloud, like asking the assistant to play the next track. Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist.
Another big capability is translation. Gemini will automatically detect languages and translate them to your preferred tongue. You do need to stare at the individual to hear their words translated, and there's a limited range; the quality depends heavily on the environment and noise level, but it worked remarkably well in my controlled demos, with only a few errors. The translation tries to mimic the speaker's tone and voice so it feels like their own words.

articles.title_orig: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.title_zh: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.content_orig:
The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied
W hat do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals , which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared.
The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. Israeli military personnel have also described the shockingly high level of civilian deaths tolerated as “collateral damage” in targeting even low-level fighters after the brutal Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.
Many more Palestinians are dying because of the war. With more than four-fifths of Gaza’s buildings destroyed, storms and the cold are proving deadly , killing at least four children and a woman last weekend. The UN says that 940,000 people are in makeshift shelters in areas at risk of flooding . Sewage is spewing into tents. In desperation, families are risking a return to ruined homes – with some dying in building collapses.
Reconstruction is the real need, but even the absolute basics are lacking: the UN says Israel is blocking 150,000 tents that are ready for use , along with other sorely needed goods, including sanitation equipment and nutrient-dense peanut butter. As an occupying power, Israel has a responsibility under international law to meet the needs of Gaza’s people. Allowing in the aid they desperately need should be the absolute minimum expected of it.
Even Donald Trump’s Netanyahu-friendly Board of Peace has urged Israel to allow in all humanitarian supplies and said that its response is insufficient – but it shows no inclination to actually use its leverage. Israel says that it has let in trucks and tents but that reconstruction can’t begin until Hamas “fully disarms”.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the military, has six weeks to form a government following elections last month, in which Benjamin Netanyahu lost his mandate. Substantial improvements are unlikely even if Mr Eisenkot succeeds; the fate of civilians in Gaza was more of an issue in the US midterms than in the Israeli election.
But as Israel gradually begins to digest the extraordinary shift in international opinion underlined by the US midterms – with about three in 10 Americans now believing that it has committed genocide – other governments have a fresh opportunity to press for change. They must use not just words but deeds. Mr Netanyahu has suggested that Israel could become an isolated “super-Sparta” . Yet it is dependent – for security, trade and diplomatically – on the US and Europe.
Other nations must also pay up: shockingly, the World Food Programme said last month that it has had to cut the number of people it can help by half a million because funding has slumped. Israel’s obstruction increases the cost of relief, and its barring of aid groups is another obstacle. Now is the time to exert maximum pressure to ensure that Palestinians can survive this winter – and that they have a future worth living for.

articles.title_orig: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

articles.title_orig: Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Before Megaspeed, there was Supermicro: The other Nvidia partner tied to China chip smuggling—and to Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit
articles.title_zh: The planet ‘is being killed’, Greta Thunberg tells Cop31 climate summit
articles.content_orig:
Swedish activist criticised world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown
The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg , who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years.
Thunberg , 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis.
“It [Earth] is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg said.
“No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”
Thunberg, who in recent years has shifted her focus towards other areas such as the conflict in Gaza , linked worsening global heating to other calamities such as war in an appearance alongside activists from Nepal, Canada and Australia.
“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” she said.
“It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.”
The intervention, on the fourth day of the two-week summit, came as world leaders who travelled to the Mediterranean coastal city delivered their own verdicts on the climate crisis and the faltering progress to address it.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, who was the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said in a speech that the record hot summer in the UK was “not normal”.
“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” said Burnham, who promised the UK would get to net zero emissions, and backed a proposal for countries to further electrify their economies.
Beth John, a climate justice adviser at Oxfam GB, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”. But she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.”
The electrification goal is one of the main potential promises expected at the talks, which are being jointly presided over by Turkey and Australia. Some countries want the agreement text to specify that the electricity will be derived from clean energy sources.
Campaigners have criticised governments for their slow pace of emissions cuts and for, so far, failing to rally around a phaseout of fossil fuels in the negotiations.
Current policies are set to heat the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, a report by Climate Action Tracker found on Thursday. The catastrophic rise in temperatures is slightly more than the group expected last year and well above the 1.5C that world leaders have promised.
Thursday was rife with accounts of the harm caused by the climate crisis. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, recounted the disastrous landslide – caused by a melting glacier – that struck the country in August, claiming more than 1,500 lives.
after newsletter promotion
“We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,” Chaudhary told the Guardian. “We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.”
In the main conference room, a speech by Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, drew a standing ovation from delegates as he described the environmental impact of the three-year war with Israel.
“Israel’s restrictions on access to land, water and natural resources have compounded Palestine’s climate challenges,” said Mustafa, who spelled out how widespread destruction in Gaza, including to water supplies, sewerage and farmland, had worsened environmental and health risks.
The Turkish hosts of Cop31 have repeatedly accused Israel of genocide and refused to invite the country’s leadership to Antalya. Israel denies that it has committed genocide and insists it has fought a legitimate war to safeguard its own security.
Another country not formally present at the talks is the US, which did not send a delegation. Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the international climate framework, derided climate science as a “hoax”, and claimed he would not permit any new wind turbines.
This stance earned a rebuke from John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, who has made the trip to Turkey along with 20 Democratic members of Congress and two state governors. “He’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues,” Kerry said of Trump in response to a question from the Guardian.
The crushing midterm election win by the Democrats has raised hopes here at Cop of the US re-engaging on the climate crisis. But Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, warned the final two years of the Trump presidency would not see fundamental change on climate policy.
“I don’t want to romanticise what this will mean,” Newsom said on Thursday. “I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down.”

articles.title_orig: Retail investors are buying Nvidia’s stock crash like never before — history urges patience
articles.title_zh: Retail investors are buying Nvidia’s stock crash like never before — history urges patience
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6.
It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership.
"The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable."
While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says.
Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says.
In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy.
When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management.
Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?"
If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount.
"If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs."
Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says.
And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability.
"Did Nvidia's prospects change as a result of [Huang's resignation]? There's no definitive answer for that," he says.
Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund's fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. Even companies that have successfully replaced their founders, such as Apple and Microsoft , have failed to grow as quickly as under original leadership, he says.
Investors will have to weigh the risk that Nvidia will lag without Huang at the helm against the firm's still impressive growth projections — the company will report third-quarter fiscal year earnings results on Nov. 17 — and their long-term belief in the firm's position as a top supplier of microchips that power AI.
"One thing we do know is that AI demand hasn't changed," Hainlin says.

articles.title_orig: Sheinbaum to address APEC business leaders in China: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
articles.title_zh: Sheinbaum to address APEC business leaders in China: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
articles.content_orig:
President Sheinbaum’s agenda in China next week was a key focus of today’s mañanera .
Sheinbaum will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting in the southeastern Chinese city of Shenzhen next Wednesday and Thursday.
She announced last week that she will also attend a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
On Thursday morning, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard provided an overview of Sheinbaum’s agenda in China.
He and other cabinet ministers, including Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco, will accompany the president on her trip to China, her first to Asia since she was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024.
The focus on Sheinbaum’s upcoming trip at today’s mañanera served as a reminder that Mexico has taken a more prominent place on the international stage under her leadership than it occupied during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency. AMLO only took seven international trips during his six-year term, a number matched by Sheinbaum before she reached the two-year milestone of her presidency .
In addition to attending the APEC meeting in China next week, Sheinbaum will also travel to Florida next month to attend the G20 Leaders’ Summit. At today’s mañanera , she said that her first formal face-to-face meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump could take place at the latter event.
Ebrard told reporters that Sheinbaum will have official activities scheduled in Shenzhen from Nov. 17 to 19.
He noted that Shenzhen is considered the technology capital of China.
“That’s why they proposed holding [the APEC meeting] there,” Ebrard said.
He announced that Sheinbaum will be the main speaker at an APEC Business Advisory Council event to be held in Shenzhen next week. Ebrard said that the council is made up of “more than 1,000 businesspeople from the 21 [APEC] countries.”
“We think that this is the most important [business] forum for … the Asia-Pacific [region] and our president is going to play a very important role,” he said.
“She will be one of the few heads of state that will address the group in the plenary session,” Ebrard said.
In fact, just Sheinbaum and Xi will address the session attended by all members of the APEC Business Advisory Council, he said.
Ebrard also announced that Sheinbaum will hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of various APEC countries, including those of China, Canada, Australia and Vietnam. He said that other APEC countries have requested bilateral meetings with Mexico, and that it is “very likely” they will take place. Ebrard said that leaders of APEC countries have significant interest in “talking to the president and Mexico.”
He said that Sheinbaum will also participate in the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. Ebrard noted that the theme of this year’s meeting is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together.”
He subsequently told reporters that 52% of foreign direct investment in Mexico comes from APEC countries. Ebrard also noted that Mexico will host the APEC Leaders’ Meeting in 2028.
Later in the press conference, Sheinbaum told reporters that she won’t hold a bilateral meeting with Trump during her visit to China next week.
She said she would “probably” meet with the U.S. president during the G20 Leaders’ Summit at the Mar-A-Lago Club in Florida in December.
“We will seek … [a bilateral meeting] if the opportunity arises,” Sheinbaum said.
She emphasized that there is constant communication between Mexico and the United States on trade issues.
Sheinbaum said last week that she was interested in meeting with Trump in China.
Sheinbaum told reporters that she will speak about Plan México — the federal government’s ambitious economic plan — at the APEC Business Advisory Council event.
“We’re going to talk about Plan México, about what we’ve done , about what our country’s economic model means,” she said.
Sheinbaum wants to make Mexico 10th largest economy in the world with ‘Plan México’
Sheinbaum said she will also speak to businesspeople about how they can invest in Mexico.
Among the goals of Plan México are to attract more foreign investment to Mexico and to increase the use of national content in products made in Mexico’s large manufacturing sector.
“The objective of Plan Mexico is to produce more in Mexico and import less,” Sheinbaum told reporters.
Sheinbaum told reporters that there is no reason why her meeting with Xi should affect Mexico’s trade negotiations with the United States.
“That we’re going to have a meeting with the president of China shouldn’t be a problem in the trade agreement negotiations with the United States,” she said.
Mexico and the United States have been seeking to resolve a range of trade differences after the Trump administration announced in July that it had decided against renewing the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years to 2042.
The United States’ concerns include its large trade deficit with Mexico , Mexico’s trade relationship with China and Mexico’s energy sector rules . Mexico is seeking a reduction, if not the elimination, of U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

articles.title_orig: Mortgage Rates Remain High as Affordability Challenges Persist
articles.title_zh: Mortgage Rates Remain High as Affordability Challenges Persist
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remain above 7 percent, adding pressure to a bleak housing market struggling with rising prices and declining sales.
The rate on the most popular home loan in the United States, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, fell slightly to 7.11 percent, from 7.18 percent the week before, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. The same rate averaged 6.24 percent a year ago.
There was hope that mortgage rates might ease below 7 percent, a psychological threshold that could draw more buyers to the market. But industry experts say that marker is not likely to be breached any time soon.
High housing costs have made buying a home unaffordable for many Americans, said Brad Case, the chief residential economist at Homes.com, a real estate search portal owned by CoStar, a data analytics company.
“I don’t think affordability challenges are going away any time soon,” he added, “because I don’t think we’re likely to see substantially lower mortgage rates.”
Squeezed by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, buyers and sellers are sitting out of the market until conditions improve, which has depressed home sales. Sales of existing homes fell 8.8 percent in October from the year before, and 5.5 percent lower than September’s pace, according to a report released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock falls after Huang resigns, weighing on broader market
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock falls after Huang resigns, weighing on broader market
articles.content_orig:
Major stock indexes closed slightly lower following news that Jensen Huang, one of the most important executives in the AI boom, was resigning effective immediately as CEO of Nvidia.
After diving as much as 16%, Nvidia’s stock ended the day down by 4.3%, as the company and investors grappled with multiple scandals that have engulfed its co-founder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
Throughout the day, the company was among the biggest decliners on the Nasdaq and S&P 500 indexes. It was the biggest decliner on the Dow.
Without a formal succession plan, Nvidia, which designs the chips powering the entire AI sector, was thrust into crisis. It’s a pivotal moment for AI, with Anthropic gearing up for its potentially trillion-dollar-plus initial public offering next week.
Anthropic is highly reliant on Nvidia’s chips and has entered into hundreds of billions of dollars worth of contracts with cloud providers to rent them.
Nvidia named its longtime chief financial officer as its interim leader. Huang’s departure from Nvidia came after a New York Times report said the CEO had had a relationship with an executive at Nvidia who reports to him.
That came right on the heels of his admission Sunday that he was “unfaithful” to his wife, an announcement that was released after the Financial Times reported Saturday that Huang had had a relationship with a businesswoman whom a source told NBC News was a Chinese spy.
There are few companies as important to the artificial intelligence industry as Nvidia.
“We’re probably the only AI company in the world that works with every AI company in the world,” Huang told Bloomberg in an October interview.
As reports swirled around Huang this week, Nvidia’s shares have plunged, erasing about $500 billion in value. Nvidia’s total market value fell below $4 trillion for the first time since 2025 in early trading. It ended the day barely above that level.
The news surrounding Huang, a confidant of President Donald Trump’s, also raises the prospect of tighter regulations on the chip and AI industry, which could further pressure stock indexes that have been powered for years by the explosion in AI stocks.
“All told, given the national security concerns, we think the risk of more restrictive guidelines on shipments directly or indirectly into China has risen,” JPMorgan analysts said Thursday before Huang was removed.
Industry experts widely believe that American leadership in AI has been powered by Nvidia. That too could come into question.
“We expect the [Nvidia] team to maintain its leadership in AI,”  JPMorgan’s team said, while cautioning that “history has shown that one execution misstep often leads to more.”
“Maintaining flawless execution” will be critical to Nvidia and the sector going forward, they said.
Also pressuring stock indexes was news from AI cloud startup Nebius, which reported that it beat earnings expectations. But the company also gave investors disappointing guidance.
Investors have been on edge about AI-linked firms, especially smaller startups, given that they require tens of billions of dollars to get their data centers up and running. Overall, the sector has poured hundreds of billions of dollars into developing AI systems, data centers and equipment, but investors remain nervous about how soon those investments could pay off.
Nebius shares plummeted 17%. Its data center peer CoreWeave also fell 7% after surging Wednesday.
Suppliers to both companies also fell. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell 0.5%, while an ETF that tracks memory suppliers fell 2.6%.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Why Trump thinks tiny trucks could solve car affordability crisis
articles.title_zh: Why Trump thinks tiny trucks could solve car affordability crisis
articles.content_orig:
Imagine a pickup truck, but much smaller, lighter and lacking any frills. It’s a vehicle that people in Japan have been using for decades. And now Toyota wants to sell one in the United States.
This week, the automaker introduced a tiny pickup truck inspired by Japanese “Kei” trucks, under the Scion brand that Toyota shuttered in 2016. The vehicle, the Scion KEI-01, will go on sale next year.
Kei vehicles (pronounced like the letter “K”) are a distinct category of small cars, vans and trucks in Japan and other Asian countries. These vehicles have long had a cult following in the United States. Even President Trump showed adoration , calling them “really cute” and “sort of like the Beetle used to be.” He made the remarks last year after a visit to Japan and mused about finding a way to have them sold in the United States.
But buying and using one of these vehicles in the United States is not easy. Car buffs who want Kei cars and trucks typically import vehicles that are at least 25 years old from Japan to take advantage of a provision in U.S. law that exempts older vehicles from federal safety and emissions standards.
Toyota says the KEI-01 will be assembled in Indiana and will qualify as a “low speed vehicle” under federal regulations. Vehicles in that category must have a top speed of 25 miles an hour and are generally forbidden from roads with speed limits of more than 35 m.p.h. Such vehicles also do not have to meet the same safety and other standards as regular cars.
The KEI-01 is in many ways the opposite of traditional U.S. pickup trucks like the Ford F-150 or Chevrolet Silverado, which over the past several decades have become bigger, heavier and more expensive. Most automakers have found that it is much easier to make a profit on larger vehicles because they tend not to cost much more to make than smaller ones but can be sold for a lot more money.

articles.title_orig: Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal | Blogs | Nov 12, 2026 - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.title_zh: Don't Let China's Espionage Become America's Own Goal | Blogs | Nov 12, 2026 - Information Technology and Innovation Foundation
articles.content_orig:
An alleged Chinese intelligence operation targeting Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang could end up costing the United States far more than it costs China. Nvidia has lost its longtime chief executive, American investors have lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value, and U.S. policymakers are considering new restrictions on chip exports that could further undermine American technology companies. The United States has a legitimate interest in preventing the Chinese military from acquiring advanced AI chips, but it should not allow an alleged Chinese espionage operation to push it toward policies that weaken its own semiconductor industry.
The controversy began with reports that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, of working for China's Ministry of State Security. Investigators reportedly suspected she had cultivated a relationship with Jensen Huang to gather information about Nvidia and its operations. Jensen Huang acknowledged having an extramarital relationship with her and separately faced reports of another relationship with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. On November 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO after 33 years leading the company and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
The allegations raise serious national security concerns. Megaspeed reportedly purchased approximately $4.8 billion in Nvidia hardware . U.S. authorities suspected that the company was helping Chinese customers circumvent restrictions on advanced AI chips. During a 2024 inspection of a Malaysian facility, Commerce Department officials reportedly found Nvidia hardware still packed in boxes rather than installed in data centers, raising concerns that the equipment might be destined for China.
These allegations remain under investigation. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing, says it is cooperating with inspections by U.S. authorities, and has commissioned an independent review by a U.S. law firm of its chip inventory and export-control practices. Singaporean authorities are also investigating the company.
If the allegations are true, China will have achieved something significant: disrupting one of America's most important technology companies and potentially gaining access to sensitive commercial information. Even without evidence that Nvidia's trade secrets or national security information were compromised, the damage is already substantial. Nvidia has lost its longtime leader, its shareholders have seen hundreds of billions of dollars in market value evaporate, and the company faces renewed uncertainty about its ability to serve international customers. The immediate economic costs are falling on an American company and its investors.
China's own semiconductor strategy makes the situation particularly revealing. Beijing wants to reduce dependence on American technology and build a domestic chip industry. It has increasingly used procurement restrictions and government guidance to steer Chinese companies toward domestic processors. In November 2025, for example, Chinese authorities reportedly directed state-funded data centers to use domestically produced AI chips . In January 2026, Chinese authorities also discouraged purchases of Nvidia's H200 processors, despite strong interest from Chinese companies.
Yet Chinese companies continue to seek access to Nvidia's most powerful processors, including through overseas data centers. This reflects a distinction between Beijing's long-term industrial ambitions and the immediate commercial interests of Chinese technology companies. China wants its domestic chipmakers to capture the market, but its AI developers still benefit from access to the best available hardware.
Congress now risks helping China achieve its goals. One proposal, the Remote Access Security Act (RASA) , would expand export controls to cover foreign access to restricted U.S. technology through cloud computing services. The legislation addresses a legitimate concern: Chinese companies could potentially rent computing capacity overseas even when they cannot legally purchase the underlying chips. But an overly broad law could also create uncertainty for legitimate international cloud services and impose new compliance costs on American technology companies.
The AI OVERWATCH Act and Chip Security Act would go further. The AI OVERWATCH Act would require licenses for certain advanced-chip exports to countries of concern and give Congress advance notice of proposed sales, with an opportunity to block them through a joint resolution. That process could make access to U.S. chips subject to greater political uncertainty, even for transactions that meet existing export-control requirements. The Chip Security Act would require security mechanisms to help verify whether exported chips have been diverted, potentially including location trackers, on-site audits, or legal attestations. Such measures could help detect illicit transfers, but they could also raise concerns among legitimate international customers about monitoring, data security, and government access to information about their computing infrastructure. Both bills risk making U.S. technology less attractive to customers who have other options.
The United States should strengthen enforcement against companies and individuals that knowingly divert restricted chips. It should also improve verification of end users and investigate suspicious transactions. But Congress should be careful about creating new restrictions that unnecessarily limit legitimate commercial activity.
American semiconductor leadership depends heavily on private-sector investment in research and development. Nvidia and other U.S. chipmakers spend billions developing successive generations of increasingly powerful processors. International sales generate revenue that supports this investment, helps companies achieve economies of scale, and finances future innovation. Overly restricting access to the Chinese market would weaken an important source of commercial demand while giving Chinese competitors more opportunities to improve their products and gain market share.
China has an obvious interest in reducing its dependence on American semiconductors. But its own record of economic espionage and trade-secret theft—including documented efforts to steal semiconductor technology —underscores why the allegations deserve serious attention. President Trump should put the issue on the agenda when he meets Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen later this month.
Any proven violations should carry meaningful consequences. But a domestic response that hurts American companies, reduces their global markets, and encourages customers to adopt Chinese alternatives would compound the damage. China may have played Jensen Huang. Congress should make sure it does not play into Beijing's hands.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: US DOJ probes Nvidia as fallout from Huang’s resignation ripples across Washington
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: US DOJ probes Nvidia as fallout from Huang’s resignation ripples across Washington
articles.content_orig:
"I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
Republican lawmakers are continuing to call for testimony from Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday morning following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
GOP Rep. Tim Burchett said it was a "good move" for Huang to resign, adding that the former Nvidia executive should testify as lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Burchett said to reporters at the Capitol Thursday morning.
Rep. John Moolenaar, the chairman of the China Select Committee, told ABC News that lawmakers have growing concerns as details of Huang's affair continue to come to light.
"The concerns are our national security, whether he was being influenced by a Chinese spy, and the Chinese intelligence was gathering information about our crown jewels of American technology, and also this issue of chip diversion," said Moolenaar, who added that he would support a congressional subpoena to compel Huang's testimony.
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Brian Mast and Moolenaar both say that they're still in active conversations with Huang to schedule testimony after the former Nvidia CEO had previously signaled a willingness to testify.
"We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us. If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power," Moolenaar said.
Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte said he believes that Huang's affair is a distraction.
"I hope we can keep the conversation centered around the pros and cons of our export policy regarding our most advanced chips, and you know, not talk about, you know, personal peccadillos,” Obernolte said.
Before Huang's resignation, lawmakers had called for him to testify. Last week, GOP Reps. Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and Moolenaar sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing." Moolenaar said Huang responded to that letter and they are discussing a "date that works."
Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Jensen Huang has not responded to ABC News' previous requests for comment about testifying on Capitol Hill. ABC News is working to contact Huang on Thursday -- after he left Nvidia.
On the Democratic side, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media on Thursday morning that despite Huang's resignation, Congress needs more answers from Huang, Nvidia and the administration.
"Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote.
Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons are asking the White House and the Departments of Commerce and State to preserve all documents related to the export of NVIDIA's advanced AI chips to China following reports that some senior officials were aware that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spying operation. The two senators wrote a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Wednesday.
Coons and Warren are also requesting preservation of all materials related to the reported intelligence operation and for a briefing to members of Congress.
Some Republicans have brushed aside concerns, however, when asked whether Huang's access to President Donald Trump at state dinners and flying on Air Force One was problematic given his affair with an alleged Chinese spy was purportedly known to the intelligence community.
"I'm not concerned about -- about Jensen's access to the president. I'm sure the president can take care of that," Obernolte said.
Republicans have said they are hoping to bring in Huang before handing over majority control to Democrats in January.
"You know, it's obviously -- with him resigning -- that does change the dynamic," Moolenaar said. "He has stated he's a patriot. He has questioned people who viewed export controls as a sound policy. I would hope he would want to come in and have that discussion with us."
ABC News' Allison Pecorin contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
articles.title_zh: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
articles.content_orig:
Kelly Clancy speaks at a protest against Google's AI in New York City public schools. Alex Nguyen
Parents, students, educators, union members, artists , creatives , and community members stood outside Google’s New York City headquarters, located in the eerie corporate section of Manhattan’s Hudson Square neighborhood on Wednesday afternoon to protest Google pushing its AI technology into schools.
It was a family event: Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.
Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.
Rallies also took place on Wednesday in six other cities —Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—organized by a nationwide alliance of parent advocacy organizations.
Just over a week earlier, on Election Day, Google announced that it would turn off its AI tools for school systems unless administrators choose to turn them on. But among these AI tools is Google Search, which has become synonymous with how to seek information on the internet. With New York City enacting a one-year AI moratorium on generative AI use for many elementary and middle school students, schools would lose Google’s search capacity entirely. Some other major public school systems, like the Los Angeles Unified School District , have also widely limited student access to generative AI on school devices.
Both New York City and Los Angeles are Google clients. In an effort to quickly set up remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic, many school districts invested in Google Chromebooks , which were notably more affordable than Windows and Apple computers. Incorporating Chromebooks in the classroom—and according to what some parents told me, into homes where many students use them for homework—is pervasive, as these schools integrate the hardware with Google Classroom, which manages assignments, posts announcements, syncs with Google Calendar and Google Drive, and includes built-in AI tools through Google Gemini.
The day after Google’s announcement, Google became the subject of a lawsuit alleging that the Gemini chatbot accessed through her school-issued Chromebook diagnosed Emma, a 13-year-old girl in North Carolina, with severe psychological disorders, and assisted her in planning her suicide and funeral over a span of several months—allegedly coaching her to conceal self-harm from her family and friends. (The school’s monitoring systems reportedly flagged the activity eventually to a former school counselor who had left nine months prior. The school alerted Emma’s parents, who intervened.)
A Google spokesperson told Gizmodo last week that the firm was taking the lawsuit’s allegations “very seriously.”
“We’ve worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts,” the spokesperson added. “When people’s queries indicate they may be experiencing a crisis we show hotline information directly in Search to connect them with real-world support.”
Kelly Clancy, a parent of three, organizes with a coalition calling for a two-year pause on all generative AI in New York City’s K-12 public schools to allow time for a research-backed process to evaluate the roles AI products should have. She told me that she logged in to her kids’ school-issued Google profiles with her own computer to test what they were allowed to access. According to Clancy, students can still access Gemini on tablets and phones at school, which reverts to Google’s AI chat.
“When my son typed ‘AI sucks’—because he’s 12—it started behaving as a companion bot, telling him it was here to listen and that it heard him,” Clancy said.
Craig, a parent with a daughter in second grade in Brooklyn, said on Wednesday that while Google’s tech poses wider problems—such as consuming more energy than entire countries and driving up carbon emissions with data centers—ordinary people can still “quit using Google products.”
Shan, a former teacher and mom to a fourth grader, organizes in New York City with Schools Beyond Screens , a national coalition of parents and educators pushing for evidence-based limits on digital technology in classrooms. She said she circulated a petition that now has over 600 signatures to that effect. One question parents raised: “Why are we trusting and enabling billionaires with our children’s education, with their futures?”
At Wednesday’s protest, New York State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said he was “radicalized” when his kids entered school. Gounardes proposed the Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens (FOCUS) Act, where schools would largely be required to offer screen-free learning to students from pre-K to fifth grade.
Naveed Hasan , an elected member of New York City’s board of education, told me that the groundwork for problems with AI tech in schools came when Mayor Mike Bloomberg took control over the city’s public school system from the state government in 2002, abolishing boards that govern the city’s 32 community school districts and creating a “top-down system.”
“There’s no way that one person can direct 900,000 students worth of policy. We have dozens of neighborhoods with different ethnicities and languages, wants and needs,” Hasan said, arguing that schools need to be allowed “some freedom to do the thing they need to do for their communities.”
Sophie Hurwitz and Schuyler Mitchell

articles.title_orig: Two men guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target journalists and lawyer
articles.title_zh: Two men guilty of spying for Iran over plan to target journalists and lawyer
articles.content_orig:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets
Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.
These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.
The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.
Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.
Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.
Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.
Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
after newsletter promotion
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.
He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.
Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.
Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.
Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.
It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

articles.title_orig: House Foreign Affairs chair: ‘Very likely’ chips restrictions make it into defense bill
articles.title_zh: House Foreign Affairs chair: ‘Very likely’ chips restrictions make it into defense bill
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - US lawmakers from both parties are pushing for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced artificial intelligence chips following media reports about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which has increased scrutiny of the company's ‌role in US national security.
Huang stepped down on Thursday, days after reports of an affair with an executive at a Singapore-based tech company whom ‌US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Nvidia did not address Huang's actions in its statement; he has admitted to an extramarital affair without naming the person.
Nvidia's advanced AI chips are widely ​used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US for years has sought to limit China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, though Chinese companies have repeatedly found ways around those restrictions. Huang supported allowing more exports to China.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Thursday that the growing consensus in Congress favors new restrictions on chip exports to China.
Here are the proposals Congress is weighing. A handful of lawmakers want to ‌attach them to the annual defense authorization bill, a must-pass ⁠measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support. A Senate version of the legislation already includes several of them, including the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act and Match Act.
GROWING CONGRESSIONAL AUTHORITY OVER CHIP EXPORTS
US law gives the Commerce Department ⁠broad authority to block or allow advanced chip exports without congressional input.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, and Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, argue export-control decisions with major national security implications should face greater congressional oversight.
Their proposed AI Overwatch Act would give Congress a larger role in reviewing changes to export rules. The measure is significant for ​Nvidia ​because it could make it harder for future administrations to loosen restrictions on sales of ​its advanced chips to China.
Nvidia's revenue from chip sales to ‌Chinese data centers for now is near zero, according to an August company statement, and the company doesn't expect that to change in the third quarter.
The Chip Security Act seeks to address a recurring problem of advanced chips legally sold abroad but later diverted to China.
The bill would require chipmakers to track the location of advanced AI processors and notify the government if they suspect chips have reached prohibited users.
For Nvidia, the measure could create new compliance costs and reporting obligations. The Semiconductor Industry Association, whose members include Nvidia, has said mandatory tracking requirements could be costly for the industry.
The Match Act would ‌pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China.
Allies ​such as the Netherlands and Japan are home to ASML and Tokyo Electron , which make tools used ​to manufacture semiconductors.
The bill would not directly restrict Nvidia's chip sales. Supporters ​argue it could make it more difficult for China to develop its own advanced AI chips to compete with Nvidia in ‌the long term.
The Remote Access Security Act targets a ​growing workaround used by Chinese AI companies.
Instead ​of purchasing advanced chips directly, some Chinese firms rent computing power from overseas data centers equipped with Nvidia chips and access the systems remotely.
The bill would give the Commerce Department authority to regulate that activity. The legislation passed the House in January and is awaiting Senate consideration.
Among the proposals ​under consideration, this could have the most direct effect ‌on Nvidia. The company said in July that the measure, if enacted, could have "a material impact on our business."
Reuters reported on Thursday ​that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure access to Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China, on concerns that the controversy surrounding Huang could ​accelerate Washington's effort to tighten restrictions.
(Reporting by Courtney Rozen; editing by David Gaffen)

articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s next move is chasing the unprecedented ‘holy grail’ of rocketry. Here’s what’s at stake
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s next move is chasing the unprecedented ‘holy grail’ of rocketry. Here’s what’s at stake
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX ( SPCX +0.14% ) wants to get its whole rocket home. On Starship's 15th test flight, set for as early as Friday, Nov. 13, the company plans to catch both halves of the rocket using its launch tower. If both catches work, SpaceX says it'd be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system.
The bottom half, the Super Heavy booster, has been caught on three past test flights. The top half hasn't. That part's the upper stage (the section that takes satellites the rest of the way to orbit, which SpaceX simply calls the ship).
Since its IPO , SpaceX's stock has traded as high as $225.64. Shares trade around $143 as I write, about 37% under that high. With a potentially historic flight a day away, is the stock a buy?
I think a successful catch would be a big milestone for Starship. But I doubt it would change much about what investors are paying for now.
Image source: Getty Images.
SpaceX's mission page shows a 75-minute launch window starting at 4:45 p.m. Central time on Friday, pending regulatory approval as I write. The booster is due to be caught around six and a half minutes after liftoff. The ship, meanwhile, is meant to deploy 26 of Starlink's bigger V3 satellites and spend over 22 hours in orbit before trying to land at the tower in Texas. If Starship takes off on Friday, that would put the ship's catch on Saturday afternoon.
Even that final step isn't a given. SpaceX said the ship will only come back to the launch site if its flight control team confirms that the systems it needs for reentry and landing are healthy. Otherwise, it can be brought down over the ocean instead.
"Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," CEO Elon Musk said on the Oct. 20 earnings call.
A rocket that returns can fly again. On the same call, President Gwynne Shotwell said SpaceX's aim is to "refly the second stage by early next year." Reusing the ship is what's meant to change Starship from an expensive test program into a far cheaper way to reach orbit.
For now, the program is still getting more expensive. Showing how hard SpaceX is pushing, the space segment's research and development spending grew 44% year over year to $1.2 billion in the third quarter. According to SpaceX's quarterly filing, that spending mostly goes to developing, building, and testing Starship. And it's risen every quarter this year, from $930 million in the year's first quarter to around $1.1 billion in the June quarter.
Still, the segment nearly broke even. More customer launches helped drive space revenue up 84% sequentially to $1.8 billion, and the segment's operating loss shrank to $7 million from $542 million in the second quarter.
But a year before the same segment turned a $259 million operating profit.
The bigger payoff from a reusable ship could arguably show up in Starlink. SpaceX's own payloads made up 358 of the 476 metric tons it sent to orbit in the third quarter. Plus, SpaceX says the 26 V3 satellites on Starship's first orbital flight added around 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch.
SpaceX's valuation is around $1.9 trillion at the current price. Even annualizing its third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, the shares trade at around 33 times sales.
And most of that revenue has little to do with Starship now. The super intelligence segment, SpaceX's artificial intelligence (AI) business, pulled in $7.6 billion last quarter, around half the total. Connectivity, home to Starlink, added $5.2 billion. The space segment's $1.8 billion was around 12%.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/12/26
So, a catch would likely help the long-term case more than the next few quarters. Starship still needs to fly again, fly often (Musk said on the call he expects weekly flights sometime in the first half of next year), and show lower costs in the numbers.
Sure, a miss or a delay probably wouldn't hurt today's business much. After all, Falcon 9 already launches Starlink satellites. A setback could mainly cost time and more quarters of growing Starship spending.
Is SpaceX stock a buy ahead of Friday's launch? Not for a tower landing alone, in my view. At around 33 times sales, the growth stock 's price depends mainly on AI computing and Starlink, and the Starship tab is still rising.
I wouldn't buy shares just ahead of the flight.
